title: Trending — Work from Home and Disability Employment
one_line: Using occupation-level variation in post-pandemic remote work, the authors estimate that the fourfold rise in work from home causally drove most of the 14% surge in full-time employment for people with physical disabilities in the US.
key_claims: A 1 percentage point rise in within-occupation WFH increases full-time employment for physically disabled workers by 1.0%, rising to 1.3% when instrumented with the pre-pandemic Dingel–Neiman remote-feasibility index.

The post-pandemic WFH increase explains 68–85% of the rise in full-time employment for this group, with WFH going from 7% of full workdays pre-COVID to 28% by 2023 while disabled full-time employment rose ~14% (2019–2024) against flat non-disabled employment.

Triple-difference wage estimates show relative wages for disabled workers in high-WFH occupations fell 4.2% versus non-disabled peers, consistent with an outward labor supply shift rather than a demand shock.

Effects are concentrated in full-time work with no net part-time effect, consistent with part-timers scaling up hours as commuting and workplace-access frictions disappeared; full-time is 78% of disability employment.

International comparison: Australia, Canada, France and Spain saw disability employment gains averaging ~10% above non-disabled from 2019–2022, while the UK — with generous furlough schemes freezing labor reallocation — was the exception.
limitations: Analysis drops the cognitive disability category entirely (which grew by over a million people, ~6M to >7M) to avoid compositional bias, so findings speak only to the five physical categories.
WFH exposure is measured from non-disabled workers within occupations, an indirect proxy chosen to block reverse causality rather than a direct measure of disabled workers' remote access.

Identification rests on across-occupation comparisons (86 occupational codes) with controls for non-disability employment growth; residual occupation-specific shocks correlated with WFH cannot be fully excluded.
Wage evidence is indirect inference about supply versus demand from relative price movements, not direct observation of who entered the labor market or why.
CPS self-reported disability status and pandemic-era survey disruptions may introduce measurement error not addressed in the show's account.
open_questions: Do worker-level panel data confirm that entrants came from the 'not in the labor force' category specifically because remote work removed commuting or accessibility barriers?
Does the employment gain persist or reverse as firms mandate return-to-office, which would be a clean natural test of the causal claim?
Would individual-level accommodation data show that universal flexible-work defaults outperform ADA-style targeted accommodations, as the episode speculates?
Does the 4.2% relative wage decline reflect new entrants with lower prior experience rather than a pure supply shift?
